title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response & Evidence Workflows
author: Avery Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's baseline security and compliance controls for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, the secure software development lifecycle (SDLC), incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and risk & exceptions. It provides prescriptive configurations, ownership, operational runbooks and evidence collection guidance used for internal reviews and external audits.

Scope and Purpose

- Scope: Applies to all Redwood-managed control plane services, hosted tenants, Dedicated control plane components, and Private deployment reference artifacts.
- Purpose: Ensure consistent, auditable controls across environments that meet enterprise compliance (SOC2/ISO27001) requirements and customer contractual obligations.

Owner & Contacts

- Primary owner: Security Team (security@redwood.ai) — day-to-day: Avery Chen (security engineer).
- Secondary/backup: Jordan Martinez (principal security engineer).
- On-call for security incidents: PagerDuty escalation (team: security-oncall).

Key SLAs and Metrics

- Audit log ingestion latency: <= 5 minutes for production events.
- Audit log retention availability: 99.9% (logs queryable via Splunk/Datadog).
- Evidence retrieval SLA for audit requests: <= 24 hours.
- RBAC review cadence: Quarterly (90-day) entitlement reviews.

1) RBAC & Authentication

Goal: Principle of least privilege, centralized identity, time-bound elevation, and auditable entitlement changes.

Standards and Configurations

- Identity provider: Okta (SSO + SCIM for user/group provisioning). All human accounts must authenticate via Okta with MFA configured (minimum of 2 factors; hardware key for admin roles recommended).
- Service accounts: Managed through GitHub Actions OIDC where possible; otherwise use short-lived AWS/GCP service tokens and HashiCorp Vault-held credentials. No long-lived secrets in repos.
- Role model: Use coarse-grained org roles that map to fine-grained resource roles in Terraform-managed IAM. Example role mapping:
  - security-admin: full access to security tooling, audit log config, incident tooling (restricted).
  - infra-operator: deploy/manage infra, no access to customer data by default.
  - service-owner: app-level deploy and config control for a named service.
  - read-only-auditor: read-only access to metrics/logs/evidence stores.

Entitlement Management

1. Provisioning: SCIM sync from Okta -> GitHub org teams -> Terraform-managed IAM groups.
2. Approvals: All additions to privileged roles require written approval in the access request system (Jira request with approver sign-off).
3. Just-in-time elevation: Use short-lived elevation via Privileged Access Manager (PAM) for emergency tasks (max 24 hours).
4. Reviews: Quarterly entitlement review run by team leads and Security. Audit artifacts: review ticket, export of group membership (CSV), sign-off checklist.

Authentication & Secrets

- MFA required for all interactive logins.
- Passwordless / hardware token encouraged for admin roles.
- Secrets storage: HashiCorp Vault (transit + kv) or cloud KMS + encrypted S3 buckets. Keys managed with KMS rotation policy (90 days rotation for symmetric keys used in transit).

2) Audit Logging

Goal: Capture sufficient telemetry to reconstruct actions affecting customer data, privilege changes, security configuration changes, and system admin actions.

Collected Sources

- Okta system logs (authn, provisioning) 
- Cloud provider audit logs (AWS CloudTrail, GCP Audit Logs) for management plane actions
- Service-level audit events emitted by Redwood services (authz decisions, config changes, model pinning, rollout events) to the internal audit streaming topic (kafka-audit-prod)
- Application request traces forwarded to Datadog APM (sampling for performance, full traces for errors)
- Infrastructure events (k8s audit logs)

Logging Pipeline and Retention

| Source | Collector | Primary Store | Retention (prod) | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| Okta | Okta Syslog -> Fluentd | Splunk (index: okta-auth) | 2 years | Authn + provisioning events
| AWS CloudTrail | CloudTrail -> Kinesis -> Fluentd | S3 (encrypted) + Splunk | 7 years (Cloud) | Management plane actions archived to Glacier Cold after 1 year
| Application audit events | Service -> kafka-audit-prod -> Fluentd | Splunk/Elasticsearch | 5 years | PII redaction applied at producer
| K8s audit logs | Fluent Bit -> Splunk | Splunk | 2 years | Include controller/user identity

Operational Requirements

- Tamper-evidence: Write-once S3 prefixes with bucket-level logging and KMS-encrypted objects for long-term archives.
- Integrity checks: Weekly checksum verification for archived buckets.
- Alerting: Missing or delayed (>10 min) audit stream triggers high-priority PagerDuty alert to infra and security.

3) Data Residency & Retention

Principles

- Customer data residency is honored per customer contract: data at rest located only in approved regions (US, EU, APAC regions as specified).
- Default retention windows are driven by data type and contractual SLA — see table below.

Retention by Data Type

| Data Type | Default Retention (hosted) | Backup / Archive | Deletion Process |
|---|---:|---|---|
| User-generated content (prompts, documents) | 90 days (unless customer opts longer) | S3 encrypted, 1 year cold archive | Deletion job: async delete -> verification -> audit entry |
| Model artifacts (customer fine-tunes) | Customer-controlled (customer may request deletion) | 7 years | Manual deletion request + verification checklist |
| Audit logs (access/control) | 5 years (prod) | Glacier/Cold | Automated lifecycle to archive after 1 year; deletion controlled by compliance team |
| Backups (DB snapshots) | 30 days hot, 1 year cold | Encrypted storage | Retention policy enforced by terraform snapshot lifecycle |

Data Residency Controls

- Region tagging: All storage buckets and DB instances must include region tags and customer-residency labels. Terraform policies prevent cross-region replication for residency-constrained tenants.
- Data transfer: Cross-region transfers require ticketed approval and are logged as a high-sensitivity event.

Customer Data Deletion Process

1. Customer submits deletion request via support portal (flagged as high-priority).
2. Support engineers create a deletion runbook ticket (template: deletion-request-YYYYMMDD).
3. Owner runs deletion job (idempotent) against service APIs; generate proof-of-deletion artifacts (s3-listing before/after checksums).
4. Security verifies and attaches evidence to the ticket; close with customer confirmation.

4) Secure SDLC

Goals: Prevent introduction of vulnerabilities, ensure reproducible builds, and provide audit trails for code changes and deployment approvals.

Required Controls

- Repository controls: All code in GitHub Enterprise with protected branches, required code review (>=1 maintainer), and status checks passing.
- CI: GitHub Actions with mandatory checks: unit tests, integration tests, SAST (e.g., Semgrep), dependency scanning (Snyk), and secret scanning.
- Infrastructure as Code: Terraform modules stored in private registry; plan/apply split, approvals for apply in protected environments.
- Build & Signing: All production artifacts must be produced by CI and signed. No manual build uploads.
- Change windows & deploy gating: Production deploys require 2/3 approvals from service owners and a security approver for infra changes. Canary rollout (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with automated rollback on error budget breaches.

Developer Security Checklist (required in PR template)

1. Security scan results attached and explained.
2. Secrets check passed.
3. Attack surface changes (network ingress, new scopes) reviewed.
4. Rollout plan and rollback steps documented.

5) Incident Response (Security) Procedures

Classification

- Sev1-Security: Active incident impacting confidentiality or integrity of customer data or the platform (eg. data exfiltration, active exploit).
- Sev2-Security: Degraded security controls with potential impact (eg. credential leak to limited scope).
- Sev3-Security: Low risk or informational.

Response Steps (high level)

1. Triage & Containment: Security oncall paged; isolate affected systems (network ACLs, rotate keys, revoke tokens).
2. Evidence Preservation: Preserve relevant audit logs, create forensic snapshots, and copy to isolated evidence store (read-only S3 prefix with KMS key: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111122223333:key/evidence-key).
3. Investigation & Root Cause: Run timeline reconstruction using Splunk queries, k8s audit logs, and application audit events.
4. Remediation & Mitigation: Apply hotfixes, rotate secrets, and patch vulnerable components.
5. Customer Notification: If customer data affected, notify per contractual SLA and PII breach laws.
6. Post-Incident Review: Create a security postmortem, action items (owner + due date), and track remediation in the security backlog.

Forensic Evidence Collection Checklist (must be followed per incident)

- Snapshot of cloud resources (EC2/EBS/K8s pod), system logs, application audit logs, and network flow logs.
- Hash and store evidence copies in the evidence bucket with checksum and chain-of-custody metadata.
- Document who accessed evidence and when in the incident ticket.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Purpose: Ensure repeatable, auditable generation of evidence for audits (SOC2/ISO).

Evidence Types and Sources

- Policy documents: Stored in Confluence (space: security-and-compliance) with version history.
- Operational runbooks: Stored in repo under /runbooks and mirrored to Confluence.
- Entitlement exports: Quarterly CSV exported from Okta and GitHub; signed by approvers and stored in evidence store.
- Audit log extracts: Splunk saved searches with export to encrypted S3 prefix.

Evidence Collection Procedure

1. Request received: Compliance team creates ticket (template: evidence-request-YYYYMMDD).
2. Data pull: Security/Infra run saved searches and exports to S3 evidence-prefix/{request-id}/.
3. Packaging: Attach tickets, screenshots, and checksums; generate manifest.json (metadata) and sign with team GPG key.
4. Delivery: Upload manifest + artifacts to the compliance catalog and notify auditors.

Naming & Retention Conventions

- Evidence artifact naming: {yyyyMMdd}_{system}_{artifact-type}_{request-id}.{ext}  
- Storage: evidence-bucket/{year}/{request-id}/
- Retention: match artifact type; but audit evidence stored for a minimum of 7 years unless restricted by law.

7) Risk & Exceptions

Temporary Exceptions

- Exceptions are permitted only following a documented risk assessment and approval by Security and a business approver. Use the exception template (Jira: security-exception-xxxx).
- Required fields: scope, duration (max 90 days), compensating controls, risk owner, and mitigations.

Approval Process

1. Requestor files the exception ticket with a technical justification and proposed mitigations.
2. Security performs risk assessment and proposes compensating controls.
3. Approvers (Security lead + Business owner) sign off.
4. Expiration: All exceptions auto-remind 14 days prior to expiry; renewals require full reassessment.

Example Exception (short)

- Title: Allow inbound SSH from partner IP for data recovery
- Duration: 14 days
- Compensating controls: IP allowlist, just-in-time VPN, privileged session recording, and post-task key rotation
- Approval: Security Lead (Avery Chen), Business Owner (S. Patel)

Appendix: Useful Commands & Links

- Okta exports: Export -> Reports -> System Log -> Saved Search -> Export CSV
- Splunk sample query: index=audit "user="{username}"" | sort - _time
- Evidence bucket ARN: arn:aws:s3:::redwood-evidence-prod
- KMS key for evidence: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111122223333:key/evidence-key
- Runbook: confluence://security-and-compliance/incident-response-playbook
